definition: Demagogue means a leader who gains power by appealing to people's prejudices.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word demagogue. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know demagogue should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The pamphlet's warning has aged well: a demagogue never argues with figures when a scapegoat stands closer to hand.
A crowd-pleaser is far milder than a demagogue: he only flatters with jokes and applause lines, no harm meant, while a demagogue turns the crowd's prejudices into his own power.
A rabble-rouser goes further than a crowd-pleaser — the crowd leaves angry and aimed at someone; the demagogue claims the most: prejudice fed steadily until it hardens into his power.

An agitator stirs discontent on purpose — strikes, marches, unrest — and the cause may even be a just one. A demagogue has no cause but himself: he feeds an audience's prejudices because prejudice, once fed, converts straight into his power.

A firebrand burns hot for a cause, honest or not — the heat is real conviction, and there is no scapegoating in it. A demagogue supplies no conviction of his own; his power is built by aiming an audience's prejudice at somebody else.

Democracy joins dem- to -cracy, "rule": rule by the people — the crowd a demagogue courts is the same demos that votes.
Demagogue means a leader who gains power by appealing to people's prejudices.
In the winter of 1936 the radio priest — the era's great demagogue — drew thirty million listeners a week.
Each program opened on a grievance his listeners nursed — lost farms, lost wages — and closed by blaming the same short list: bankers, foreigners, and whoever had doubted him that week.
He gave the air no numbers and took no questions, and any station that dropped him joined the list beside the bankers.

Demagogue is the exact word for him because it means a leader who gains power by appealing to people's prejudices — the power grows from stoking suspicions his listeners walked in carrying, not from any case he could defend.
A firebrand may burn hot for a cause; the demagogue needs your resentment of somebody else to live on.
formal / political, always disapproving
Demagogue is an accusation, not a job title — save it for leaders whose power is built on prejudice.
A loud, passionate speaker may be only a firebrand; a skilled and honest one, an orator.
And note the word's one trick: it wears this unit's de- as a costume.
Its dem- is Greek for "the people," cousin to democracy, and nothing in it is lowered or undone.

The harbor town's election had been sleepy for decades until a ferry operator named Voss began holding rallies on the pier.
He never offered a budget or a plan.
Instead, every speech circled back to the cannery workers from the neighboring valley, who, he said, were the reason wages had stalled.
The town's paper called him a demagogue, and the label fit: the resentment he stirred was not a cause he served but a ladder he climbed.
Old friends noticed he did not believe half of what he shouted.
Off the pier, he ate lunch happily beside the same valley workers he blamed at night.
By the time he won the council seat, the town had learned how cheaply fear converts into votes.
